claim: Period-2 (Per2) expression in tissues peripheral to the suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) increases during sleep deprivation in mice.
source: In the mouse, Period-2 (Per2) expression in tissues peripheral to the suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) increases during sleep deprivation
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key observation that motivates the study.

claim: Per2 expression increases at times of the day when animals are predominantly awake spontaneously.
source: In the mouse, Period-2 (Per2) expression in tissues peripheral to the suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) increases during sleep deprivation and at times of the day when animals are predominantly awake spontaneously
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key observation.

claim: The circadian sleep-wake distribution directly contributes to the daily rhythms in Per2.
source: In the mouse, Period-2 (Per2) expression in tissues peripheral to the suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) increases during sleep deprivation and at times of the day when animals are predominantly awake spontaneously, suggesting that the circadian sleep-wake distribution directly contributes to the daily rhythms in Per2.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis stated in the abstract.

claim: PER2 bioluminescence increases during spontaneous waking in freely behaving mice.
source: We found support for this hypothesis by recording sleep-wake state alongside PER2 bioluminescence in freely behaving mice, demonstrating that PER2 bioluminescence increases during spontaneous waking and decreases during sleep.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: PER2 bioluminescence decreases during sleep in freely behaving mice.
source: We found support for this hypothesis by recording sleep-wake state alongside PER2 bioluminescence in freely behaving mice, demonstrating that PER2 bioluminescence increases during spontaneous waking and decreases during sleep.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Daily recurring sleep deprivations temporarily reinstate PER2-bioluminescence rhythmicity in behaviorally arrhythmic SCN-lesioned mice.
source: The temporary reinstatement of PER2-bioluminescence rhythmicity in behaviorally arrhythmic SCN-lesioned mice submitted to daily recurring sleep deprivations substantiates our hypothesis.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: PER2 dynamics can be described by a damped harmonic oscillator driven by a sleep-wake-dependent force and an SCN-independent circadian force.
source: Mathematical modeling revealed that PER2 dynamics can be described by a damped harmonic oscillator driven by two forces: a sleep-wake-dependent force and an SCN-independent circadian force.
evidence: This is a key finding from the mathematical modeling stated in the abstract.

claim: In peripheral tissues, the clock gene circuitry integrates sleep-wake information.
source: Our work underscores the notion that in peripheral tissues the clock gene circuitry integrates sleep-wake information and could thereby contribute to behavioral adaptability to respond to homeostatic requirements.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the study's findings.

claim: The sleep-wake distribution is coordinated by the interaction of a circadian and a homeostatic process.
source: The sleep-wake distribution is coordinated by the interaction of a circadian and a homeostatic process (Daan et al., 1984).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Daan et al., 1984.

claim: Circadian rhythms in overt behavior of mammals are generated by the suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) located in the hypothalamus.
source: circadian rhythms in overt behavior of mammals are generated by the suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) located in the hypothalamus (Hastings et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Hastings et al., 2018.

claim: CLOCK/NPAS2:ARNTL (BMAL1) heterodimers drive the transcription of Period (Per1,2) and Cryptochrome (Cry1,2) genes.
source: At the molecular level, so-called 'clock genes' interact through negative transcriptional/translational feedback loops (TTFLs), where the CLOCK/NPAS2:ARNTL (BMAL1) heterodimers drive the transcription of their target genes, among them the Period (Per1,2) and Cryptochrome (Cry1,2) genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the molecular clock mechanism.

claim: PER and CRY proteins assemble into repressor complexes that inhibit CLOCK/NPAS2:ARNTL-mediated transcription.
source: Subsequently, PER and CRY proteins assemble into repressor complexes that inhibit CLOCK/NPAS2:ARNTL-mediated transcription, including their own.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the molecular clock mechanism.

claim: The molecular feedback loop present in almost each cell of the mammalian body ensures a period of ~24 hr.
source: This feedback loop, present in almost each cell of the mammalian body, interacts with other molecular pathways, together ensuring a period of ~24 hr (Hastings et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Hastings et al., 2018.

claim: The SCN synchronizes peripheral clock gene expression rhythms through its rhythmic behavioral, electrical, and humoral output.
source: The SCN synchronizes peripheral clock gene expression rhythms through its rhythmic behavioral, electrical, and humoral output generated across the day (Schibler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Schibler et al., 2015.

claim: Clock genes are involved in the homeostatic aspect of sleep regulation.
source: Accumulating evidence suggests that, perhaps surprisingly, clock genes are also involved in the homeostatic aspect of sleep regulation (Franken, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Franken, 2013.

claim: Sleep deprivation induces an increase in Per2 expression in the cerebral cortex, liver, and kidney.
source: This is illustrated by the sleep deprivation (SD)-induced increase in the expression of the clock gene Per2 in tissues peripheral to the SCN, including the cerebral cortex, liver, and kidney (Curie et al., 2013; Curie et al., 2015; Franken et al., 2007; Maret et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources (Curie et al., 2013; Curie et al., 2015; Franken et al., 2007; Maret et al., 2007).

claim: The highest level of peripheral Per2 expression is reached after the time of day mice were awake most.
source: Moreover, the highest level of peripheral Per2 expression is reached after the time of day mice were awake most, suggesting that also during spontaneous periods of waking Per2 expression accumulates.
evidence: This is an observation from previous studies that supports the hypothesis.

claim: Lesioning of the SCN attenuates the circadian amplitude of clock gene transcripts and proteins in peripheral tissues.
source: Accordingly, lesioning of the SCN, which eliminates the circadian sleep-wake distribution, attenuates the circadian amplitude of clock gene transcripts and proteins in peripheral tissues (Akhtar et al., 2002; Curie et al., 2015; Tahara et al., 2012; Saini et al., 2013; Sinturel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources (Akhtar et al., 2002; Curie et al., 2015; Tahara et al., 2012; Saini et al., 2013; Sinturel et al., 2021).

claim: Sleeping and waking are important contributors to clock gene expression.
source: Together, these studies suggest that sleeping and waking are important contributors to clock gene expression, but dissecting the contribution of the sleep-wake distribution and circadian time is challenging because the two change in parallel.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from cited studies.

claim: Per2Luc KI mice have been used to follow clock gene expression in vivo.
source: Per2Luc KI mice have been used to follow clock gene expression in vivo (Curie et al., 2015; Ohnishi et al., 2014; Tahara et al., 2012; van der Vinne et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources (Curie et al., 2015; Ohnishi et al., 2014; Tahara et al., 2012; van der Vinne et al., 2018).

claim: In previous studies using Per2Luc KI mice, mice had to be anesthetized for each measurement.
source: However, in these studies, mice had to be anesthetized for each measurement, while in the set-up used in our study (RT-Biolumicorder; Saini et al., 2013), we assessed PER2 bioluminescence continuously in freely moving mice, in central and peripheral tissues.
evidence: This contrasts previous methods with the current study's approach.

claim: The RT-Biolumicorder allows assessment of PER2 bioluminescence continuously in freely moving mice.
source: However, in these studies, mice had to be anesthetized for each measurement, while in the set-up used in our study (RT-Biolumicorder; Saini et al., 2013), we assessed PER2 bioluminescence continuously in freely moving mice, in central and peripheral tissues.
evidence: This describes the method used in the current study.

claim: The most important source contributing to the peripheral bioluminescence signals in SKH1 mice are the kidneys.
source: We established that the most important source contributing to the peripheral bioluminescence signals in the SKH1 mice are the kidneys (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by imaging data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The central bioluminescence signal obtained in B6 mice is of cortical origin.
source: We have previously shown that the central bioluminescence signal obtained in B6 mice is of cortical origin (Curie et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Curie et al., 2015.

claim: Luciferin is best delivered through implantable osmotic mini-pumps compared to administration through the drinking water.
source: Finally, by using mice expressing luciferase under the control of synthetic CAG promotor (CAG-Luc mice; Cao et al., 2004), we determined that its substrate luciferin is best delivered through implantable osmotic mini-pumps compared to administration through the drinking water.
evidence: This is a finding from pilot experiments comparing delivery methods.

claim: When luciferin is administered through drinking water, strong daily rhythms in bioluminescence are observed, likely due to rhythms in drinking behavior.
source: Under the latter condition, strong daily rhythms in bioluminescence were observed, likely as a result of rhythms in drinking behavior, thereby driving luciferin availability (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Sleep deprivation elicited a tissue-specific response in PER2 bioluminescence.
source: Similar to what was observed in that publication, SD elicited a tissue-specific response, with an immediate increase in central PER2 bioluminescence after SD, while in the periphery the response was delayed and PER2-bioluminescence increases were observed in the second and fifth hour of recovery (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1A.

claim: Central PER2 bioluminescence increased immediately after sleep deprivation.
source: Similar to what was observed in that publication, SD elicited a tissue-specific response, with an immediate increase in central PER2 bioluminescence after SD, while in the periphery the response was delayed and PER2-bioluminescence increases were observed in the second and fifth hour of recovery (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1A.

claim: Peripheral PER2 bioluminescence response to sleep deprivation was delayed, with increases observed in the second and fifth hour of recovery.
source: Similar to what was observed in that publication, SD elicited a tissue-specific response, with an immediate increase in central PER2 bioluminescence after SD, while in the periphery the response was delayed and PER2-bioluminescence increases were observed in the second and fifth hour of recovery (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1A.

claim: Sleep deprivation caused a long-term reduction of PER2 bioluminescence rhythm amplitude during recovery days.
source: In addition to these direct effects on PER2 bioluminescence within the first 6 hr of recovery, the SD also caused a long-term reduction of rhythm amplitude during both recovery days; that is, the first (REC1) and last (REC2) 24 hr period of recovery.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the effects of sleep deprivation.

claim: In the periphery, PER2-bioluminescence amplitude decreased by ca. 30% on both recovery days after sleep deprivation.
source: In the periphery, this decrease amounted to ca. 30% on both days (REC1: 17.5–41.1%; REC2: 18.7–42.4%, 95% confidence intervals [95% CI]).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: Central PER2-bioluminescence amplitude decreased significantly by 32% during the first recovery day after sleep deprivation.
source: In the central recordings, PER2-bioluminescence amplitude decreased significantly during REC1 (32% [10.2–54.5%]), whereas the decrease during REC2 (22% [0.06–44.8%]) no longer reached significance levels
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis with statistical significance.

claim: Spontaneous sustained bouts of waking were associated with increased PER2 bioluminescence.
source: Although a circadian modulation of PER2 bioluminescence of both peripheral and central origin is evident (see Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 4), we observed additional changes in bioluminescence that occurred simultaneously with changes in sleep-wake state, indicating that PER2 bioluminescence increases during wake-dominated periods and decreases during sleep-dominated periods in both tissues.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Spontaneous sustained bouts of sleep were associated with decreased PER2 bioluminescence.
source: Although a circadian modulation of PER2 bioluminescence of both peripheral and central origin is evident (see Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 4), we observed additional changes in bioluminescence that occurred simultaneously with changes in sleep-wake state, indicating that PER2 bioluminescence increases during wake-dominated periods and decreases during sleep-dominated periods in both tissues.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: At sleep-to-wake transitions, peripheral PER2 bioluminescence initially decreased after wake onset, followed by a steep increase saturating at 125%.
source: At sleep-to-wake transitions, tissue differences concerned an initial decrease in peripheral PER2 bioluminescence after wake onset, followed by a steep increase saturating at 125%.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the dynamics at sleep-wake transitions.

claim: Central PER2 bioluminescence increased from the start of waking and followed a linear time course throughout the waking period.
source: In contrast, central levels of PER2 bioluminescence increased from the start and followed a linear time course throughout the waking period.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the dynamics at sleep-wake transitions.

claim: After wake-to-sleep transitions, peripheral PER2 bioluminescence initially increased before quickly decreasing and leveling out at around 84%.
source: After wake-to-sleep transitions, peripheral PER2 bioluminescence initially increased before quickly decreasing and then leveling out at around 84% (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: After wake-to-sleep transitions, central PER2 bioluminescence decreased linearly throughout the sleep period reaching levels of 91% at the end.
source: In contrast, the central signal decreased linearly throughout the sleep period reaching levels of 91% at the end.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the dynamics at sleep-wake transitions.

claim: Changes in sleep-wake state are accompanied by physiological alterations such as changes in body and brain temperature.
source: Changes in sleep-wake state are accompanied by physiological alterations, such as changes in body and brain temperature (Sela et al., 2020; Vishwakarma et al., 2021), which could influence bioluminescence by changing substrate levels and/or the rate of the enzymatic reaction.
evidence: This is cited from Sela et al., 2020 and Vishwakarma et al., 2021.

claim: The circadian rhythms of subcutaneous temperature and PER2 bioluminescence are ca. 4 hr out of phase.
source: Although the circadian rhythms of subcutaneous temperature and PER2 bioluminescence are ca. 4 hr out of phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 6), this does not exclude the possibility that fast changes in physiology associated with sleep-wake transitions contribute to luciferin availability.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: Bioluminescence in Pkg1-Luc mice was relatively constant and did not increase at sleep-wake transitions.
source: As expected from a housekeeping gene, bioluminescence in Pkg1-Luc mice was relatively constant and did not increase at sleep-wake transitions (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: In CAG-Luc mice, bioluminescence increases at sleep-wake transitions were larger than in Per2Luc mice.
source: In contrast, in CAG-Luc mice increases at transitions were larger than in Per2Luc mice, consistent with the rapidly activated CMV-immediate-early enhancer contained within the CAG synthetic promotor (Brightwell et al., 1997; Collaco and Geusz, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5, with citations to Brightwell et al., 1997 and Collaco and Geusz, 2003.

claim: The bioluminescence changes at sleep-wake transitions are specific to the luciferase reporter construct and not an artifact of sleep-wake-related changes in physiology.
source: These results show that the bioluminescence changes at sleep-wake transitions are specific to the luciferase reporter construct and therefore not an artifact of sleep-wake-related changes in physiology.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of different luciferase constructs.

claim: Enforced wakefulness has both acute and long-term effects on PER2 bioluminescence.
source: Taken together, three observations indicate that the sleep-wake distribution importantly contributes to both central and peripheral PER2-bioluminescence dynamics: (1) enforced wakefulness has both acute and long-term effects on PER2 bioluminescence
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the study.

claim: Spontaneous waking is associated with an increase in PER2 bioluminescence.
source: (2) the changes in PER2 bioluminescence at sleep-wake transitions demonstrate that also spontaneous waking is associated with an increase, and sleep with a decrease, in PER2 bioluminescence
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the study.

claim: Sleep is associated with a decrease in PER2 bioluminescence.
source: (2) the changes in PER2 bioluminescence at sleep-wake transitions demonstrate that also spontaneous waking is associated with an increase, and sleep with a decrease, in PER2 bioluminescence
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the study.

claim: PER2 bioluminescence is high when mice are spontaneously awake more.
source: (3) that PER2 bioluminescence is high when mice are spontaneously awake more.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the study.

claim: The central PER2 bioluminescence signals tended to be noisier than peripheral signals.
source: The central PER bioluminescence signals tended to be noisier than peripheral signals (signal-to-noise ratio: –1.15 ± 1.0 and 0.37 ± 1.0 dB, respectively; estimated on 3 min values in baseline of the 6 hr SD experiments according to Leise et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of signal quality.

claim: Animals in which the SCN is lesioned (SCNx) lack a circadian organization of sleep-wake behavior under constant conditions.
source: The SCN is the main driver of the circadian sleep-wake distribution because animals in which the SCN is lesioned (SCNx) lack a circadian organization of sleep-wake behavior under constant conditions (Baker et al., 2005; Edgar et al., 1993).
evidence: This is cited from Baker et al., 2005 and Edgar et al., 1993.

claim: In behaviorally arrhythmic SCNx animals, the amplitude of clock gene expression in peripheral organs is significantly reduced, but not eliminated.
source: Under these conditions, the amplitude of clock gene expression in peripheral organs is significantly reduced, but not eliminated (Akhtar et al., 2002; Curie et al., 2015; Tahara et al., 2012; Sinturel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources (Akhtar et al., 2002; Curie et al., 2015; Tahara et al., 2012; Sinturel et al., 2021).

claim: Lesioning the SCN rendered locomotor activity arrhythmic under DD conditions.
source: Lesioning the SCN rendered LMA arrhythmic under DD conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In arrhythmic SCNx mice, rhythms in PER2 bioluminescence were strongly reduced, but not completely abolished.
source: In arrhythmic SCNx mice, we confirmed that rhythms in PER2 bioluminescence were strongly reduced, but not completely abolished (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2A–C.

claim: Repeated sleep deprivations induced a robust oscillation in the PER2-bioluminescence signal in SCNx mice.
source: The repeated SDs induced a robust oscillation in the PER2-bioluminescence signal, restoring amplitude to the levels observed prior to SCN lesioning and higher than those observed in the baseline recordings (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: The oscillation in PER2 bioluminescence continued after the end of the sleep deprivations in SCNx mice while decreasing in amplitude.
source: Importantly, the oscillation continued after the end of the SDs while decreasing in amplitude (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: The 2hOnOff protocol did not significantly decrease the ongoing circadian PER2 oscillation when analyzed at the group level.
source: Contrary to expectation, the 2hOnOff protocol did not significantly decrease the ongoing circadian PER2 oscillation when analyzed at the group level (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: Four out of six mice showed a consistent 27% reduction in PER2-bioluminescence amplitude during the 2-day 2hOnOff protocol.
source: When inspecting the individual responses, four out of the six mice did show a consistent 27% reduction (range 23–31%) in PER2-biolumininescence amplitude during the 2-day 2hOnOff protocol, while in the remaining two mice amplitude increased by 40% (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: In two out of six mice, PER2-bioluminescence amplitude increased by 40% during the 2hOnOff protocol.
source: When inspecting the individual responses, four out of the six mice did show a consistent 27% reduction (range 23–31%) in PER2-biolumininescence amplitude during the 2-day 2hOnOff protocol, while in the remaining two mice amplitude increased by 40% (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: In all six mice, PER2-bioluminescence amplitude reverted to baseline values during recovery, irrespective of whether it was increased or decreased during the 2hOnOff protocol.
source: In all six mice, PER2-bioluminescence amplitude reverted to baseline values during recovery, irrespective of whether it was increased or decreased during the 2hOnOff protocol.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the recovery after the 2hOnOff protocol.

claim: The amplitude of the circadian sleep-wake distribution decreased consistently in all mice during the 2hOnOff protocol.
source: In contrast to bioluminescence, the amplitude of the circadian sleep-wake distribution did decrease consistently in all mice (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3D and E.

claim: The circadian rhythm in the sleep-wake distribution was not eliminated during the 2hOnOff protocol.
source: The circadian rhythm in the sleep-wake distribution was, however, not eliminated because the sleep obtained during the 2 hr SDs as well as during the 2 hr SOWs both varied as a function of time of day
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the results of the 2hOnOff protocol.

claim: The model accurately captured the dynamic changes in PER2 bioluminescence in the SCNx experiment.
source: With the parameters listed in Table 1, the model captured the dynamic changes in PER2 bioluminescence in the SCNx experiment with high precision including the residual rhythmicity in baseline, the reinstated pronounced rhythmicity during the four SDs, and its subsequent dampening thereafter (Figure 4B, black line, Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4B and Table 2.

claim: The model accurately captured average bioluminescence dynamics in the 2hOnOff experiment.
source: The model also accurately captured average bioluminescence dynamics in the 2hOnOff experiment (Figure 4C, black line, Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4C and Table 2.

claim: The model accurately predicted the peripheral PER2-bioluminescence data obtained in the 6 hr SD experiment using parameters optimized for the 2hOnOff experiment.
source: To further test the performance of the model, we predicted the peripheral PER2-bioluminescence data obtained in the 6 hr SD experiment using the parameters optimized for the 2hOnOff experiment (Figure 1A, Table 1). Also, the results of this experiment could be accurately predicted with the model, including the higher PER2-bioluminescence levels reached over the initial recovery hours after SD and the subsequent longer-term reduction in amplitude (Figures 1A and 4D, Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figures 1A and 4D, and Table 2.

claim: The model could not reliably predict the central PER2-bioluminescence dynamics mainly due to an earlier phase of the central compared to the peripheral signal.
source: The model could not reliably predict the central PER2-bioluminescence dynamics mainly due to an earlier phase of the central compared to the peripheral signal (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Both forces (F→WAKE and F→PERI) are required to accurately predict PER2 dynamics under the tested experimental conditions.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that both forces are required to accurately predict PER2 dynamics under the tested experimental conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling analysis.

claim: The circadian sleep-wake organization is an important contributor to high-amplitude oscillations in PER2.
source: Therefore, the circadian sleep-wake organization is an important contributor to high-amplitude oscillations in PER2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling analysis.

claim: Per2 transcription can be initiated from its cognate E-boxes by CLOCK/NPAS2:ARNTL.
source: Per2 transcription can be initiated from its cognate E-boxes by CLOCK/NPAS2:ARNTL.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the molecular regulation of Per2.

claim: Enforced wakefulness affects the expression of other components of the TTFL besides Per2.
source: Enforced wakefulness not only affects Per2 levels but also modulates the expression of other components of the TTLF (Mang and Franken, 2015; Hor et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from Mang and Franken, 2015 and Hor et al., 2019.

claim: The SD-evoked increase in Per2 expression could be mediated through other clock genes in the circuitry.
source: The SD-evoked increase in Per2 expression could therefore be mediated through other clock genes in the circuitry, as was demonstrated by the differential SD-evoked response in Per2 levels in mice lacking the core clock genes Npas2 and both Cry1 and –2 genes (Franken et al., 2006; Wisor et al., 2002).
evidence: This is cited from Franken et al., 2006 and Wisor et al., 2002.

claim: Ligand-bound glucocorticoid receptors can induce Per2 transcription by binding to their glucocorticoid response elements.
source: For example, ligand-bound glucocorticoid receptors can induce Per2 transcription by binding to their glucocorticoid response elements (Cheon et al., 2013; So et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Cheon et al., 2013 and So et al., 2009.

claim: CREB, HSF1, and SRF can directly activate Per2 transcription through CREs, heat-shock elements, and CArG-boxes, respectively.
source: Similarly, cAMP response element (CRE)-binding protein (CREB), heat-shock factor 1 (HSF1), and serum-response factor (SRF) can directly activate Per2 transcription through CREs, heat-shock elements, and CArG-boxes, respectively, present in the Per2 gene (Gerber et al., 2013; Saini et al., 2012; Tamaru et al., 2011; Travnickova-Bendova et al., 2002).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources (Gerber et al., 2013; Saini et al., 2012; Tamaru et al., 2011; Travnickova-Bendova et al., 2002).

claim: Per2 responds to stress, light, temperature, blood-borne systemic cues, and cellular activation as an immediate early gene.
source: Through these pathways, Per2 responds to stress, light, temperature, blood-borne systemic cues, and cellular activation as an immediate early gene (IEG).
evidence: This is a summary of the various pathways that can regulate Per2.

claim: Per2 can appear rhythmic even in the absence of a functional TTFL, provided signaling pathways fluctuate cyclically.
source: Because of this, Per2 can appear rhythmic even in the absence of a functional TTFL, provided these signaling pathways fluctuate cyclically (Kornmann et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from Kornmann et al., 2007.

claim: In behaviorally arrhythmic SCNx animals, the residual PER2 rhythms might result from SCN-independent corticosterone or body temperature rhythms, or might be TTFL-driven locally.
source: In behaviorally arrhythmic SCNx animals, the residual PER2 rhythms we observed might similarly result from SCN-independent corticosterone (Andrews, 1968) or body temperature (Satinoff and Prosser, 1988) rhythms, or, alternatively, might be TTFL-driven locally (Sinturel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is speculation based on cited sources (Andrews, 1968; Satinoff and Prosser, 1988; Sinturel et al., 2021).

claim: Several pathways known to directly influence Per2 expression are activated by either spontaneous and/or enforced waking.
source: Important for the current study is that several of the pathways known to directly influence Per2 expression are activated by either spontaneous and/or enforced waking (e.g., corticosterone [Mongrain et al., 2010], temperature [Hoekstra et al., 2019], Hsf1 and Srf [Hor et al., 2019], pCREB [Cirelli and Tononi, 2000])
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources (Mongrain et al., 2010; Hoekstra et al., 2019; Hor et al., 2019; Cirelli and Tononi, 2000).

claim: A light pulse given at CT14 leads within an hour to a significant increase in Per2 transcript in the SCN.
source: For instance, a light pulse given at CT14 leads within an hour to a significant increase in Per2 transcript in the SCN (Yan and Silver, 2002).
evidence: This is cited from Yan and Silver, 2002.

claim: A large increase in hepatic Per2 transcript levels occurs within 1 hr after food presentation in fasted rats.
source: One study reported a large increase in hepatic Per2 transcript levels within 1 hr after food presentation in fasted rats (Wu et al., 2010)
evidence: This is cited from Wu et al., 2010.

claim: Light promotes Per2 translation in the SCN.
source: Per2 translation is not solely dependent on de novo transcription and, for example, in the SCN, light was shown to promote Per2 translation (Cao et al., 2015)
evidence: This is cited from Cao et al., 2015.

claim: A very fast (<30 min) 1.5-fold increase in PER2 protein is observed in fibroblasts after serum shock.
source: Such mechanism could also underlie the very fast (<30 min) 1.5-fold increase in PER2 protein observed in fibroblasts after serum shock (Cao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Cao et al., 2015.

claim: PER2 degradation is crucial in setting TTFL period and the timing and stability of the circadian sleep-wake distribution.
source: PER2 degradation is crucial in setting TTFL period and the timing and stability of the circadian sleep-wake distribution (Chong et al., 2012; D'Alessandro et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Chong et al., 2012 and D'Alessandro et al., 2017.

claim: One established pathway leading to PER2 degradation involves Casein kinase 1 (Csnk1)-mediated phosphorylation followed by the recruitment of the ubiquitin ligase β-transducin repeat-containing proteins (Btrc).
source: One established pathway leading to PER2 degradation involves Casein kinase 1 (Csnk1)-mediated phosphorylation (Eide et al., 2005) followed by the recruitment of the ubiquitin ligase β-transducin repeat-containing proteins (Btrc) (Masuda et al., 2020; Ohsaki et al., 2008; Reischl et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources (Eide et al., 2005; Masuda et al., 2020; Ohsaki et al., 2008; Reischl et al., 2007).

claim: Other kinases, such as Salt-inducible kinase 3 (Sik3), and phosphorylation-independent ubiquitin ligases, such as Transformed mouse 3T3 cell double minute 2 (Mdm2), also target PER2 for degradation.
source: Other kinases, such as Salt-inducible kinase 3 (Sik3) (Hayasaka et al., 2017), and phosphorylation-independent ubiquitin ligases, such as Transformed mouse 3T3 cell double minute 2 (Mdm2) (Liu et al., 2018, p. 2), also target PER2 for degradation.
evidence: This is cited from Hayasaka et al., 2017 and Liu et al., 2018.

claim: The SD-incurred increase in Per2 in the forebrain partly depended on glucocorticoids.
source: We already established that the SD-incurred increase in Per2 in the forebrain partly depended on glucocorticoids (Mongrain et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Mongrain et al., 2010.

claim: Restoration of daily glucocorticoid rhythms in adrenalectomized rats reinstates PER2 rhythms in several extra-SCN brain areas.
source: Along those lines, restoration of daily glucocorticoid rhythms in adrenalectomized rats reinstates PER2 rhythms in several extra-SCN brain areas (Segall and Amir, 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Segall and Amir, 2010.

claim: The large amplitude of the circadian PER2 rhythm in intact mice is likely the result of the momentum gained in the harmonic oscillator through the daily recurring sleep-wake distribution.
source: Moreover, it demonstrated that the large amplitude of the circadian PER2 rhythm in intact mice is likely the result of the momentum gained in the harmonic oscillator through the daily recurring sleep-wake distribution.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling analysis.

claim: Loss of amplitude observed at the tissue level in SCNx mice is caused by phase dispersion of the continuing rhythms in individual cells according to a currently accepted scenario.
source: This is conceptually different from a currently accepted scenario, in which direct and indirect outputs from the SCN assure phase coherence of locally generated self-sustained circadian rhythms (Schibler et al., 2015). According to this model, loss of amplitude observed at the tissue level in SCNx mice is caused by phase dispersion of the continuing rhythms in individual cells.
evidence: This is cited from Schibler et al., 2015 and contrasted with the current study's findings.

claim: Among the SCN outputs thought to convey phase coherence are feeding, locomotor activity, and changes in temperature.
source: Among the SCN outputs thought to convey phase coherence are feeding, LMA, and changes in temperature.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SCN outputs.

claim: The harmonic oscillator model showed that the sleep-wake force alone was not sufficient to predict PER2 dynamics.
source: The harmonic oscillator model further showed that, although important, the sleep-wake force alone was not sufficient to predict PER2 dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling analysis.

claim: The SCN-independent and sleep-wake-independent circadian force greatly improved the performance of the model.
source: In addition to account for the residual PER2 rhythms observed in undisturbed SCNx mice, the SCN-independent and sleep-wake-independent circadian force greatly improved the performance of the model.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling analysis.

claim: The adrenal gland can generate bona fide circadian rhythms in corticosterone release independent of the SCN.
source: Moreover, ex vivo experiments demonstrated that the adrenal gland can generate bona fide circadian rhythms in corticosterone release independent of the SCN (Andrews, 1968; Engeland et al., 2018; Kofuji et al., 2016)
evidence: This is cited from Andrews, 1968; Engeland et al., 2018; and Kofuji et al., 2016.

claim: SCNx is generally thought to abolish rhythms in circulating corticosterone levels.
source: Moreover, ex vivo experiments demonstrated that the adrenal gland can generate bona fide circadian rhythms in corticosterone release independent of the SCN (Andrews, 1968; Engeland et al., 2018; Kofuji et al., 2016), even though SCNx is generally thought to abolish rhythms in circulating corticosterone levels (Moore and Eichler, 1972).
evidence: This is cited from Moore and Eichler, 1972.

claim: Adrenalectomy was found to reduce (but not abolish) the SD-induced increase in Per2 expression in the forebrain.
source: Indeed, adrenalectomy was found to reduce (but not abolish) the SD-induced increase in Per2 expression in the forebrain (Mongrain et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Mongrain et al., 2010.

claim: Ex vivo experiments showed that periods vary among tissues and do not depend on whether tissues were obtained from an intact or SCNx mouse.
source: Ex vivo experiments showed that periods vary among tissues and do not depend on whether tissues were obtained from an intact or SCNx mouse (Cederroth et al., 2019; Yoo et al., 2004)
evidence: This is cited from Cederroth et al., 2019 and Yoo et al., 2004.

claim: Both central and peripheral PER2-bioluminescence dynamics are affected by sleep-wake state, not only after SD but also after spontaneous periods of wakefulness.
source: Our data demonstrated that both central and peripheral PER2-bioluminescence dynamics are affected by sleep-wake state, not only after SD but also after spontaneous periods of wakefulness.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: The 6 hr SD elicited an immediate increase in the central PER2 signal, while in the periphery this increase occurred several hours later.
source: Despite this general observation, we found clear tissue-specific differences: the 6 hr SD elicited an immediate increase in the central PER2 signal, while in the periphery this increase occurred several hours later, confirming our earlier findings in brain versus liver and kidney (Curie et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the text and cited from Curie et al., 2015.

claim: In the brain, PER2 bioluminescence immediately increased after the animal woke up and continued to do so until the end of the waking bout.
source: Tissue specificity was also observed after spontaneous bouts of wakefulness: in the brain, PER2 bioluminescence immediately increased after the animal woke up and continued to do so until the end of the waking bout
evidence: This is stated in the text describing tissue-specific differences.

claim: In the kidney, the increase in PER2 bioluminescence became apparent only 5–10 min after the sleep-to-wake transition.
source: whereas in the kidney the increase in PER2 bioluminescence became apparent only 5–10 min after the transition.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing tissue-specific differences.

claim: The model describes the global effects of external forces on the behavior of the oscillator, but not their acute effects.
source: In its current form, the model describes the global effects of external forces (the sleep-wake distribution and the SCN-independent circadian force) on the behavior of the oscillator, but not their acute effects.
evidence: This is a limitation of the model stated in the text.

claim: The model only makes predictions on the TTFL aspect of PER2 regulation, not on PER2 as an IEG.
source: Translated into molecular terms, the model only makes predictions on the TTFL aspect of PER2 regulation, not on PER2 as an IEG.
evidence: This is a limitation of the model stated in the text.

claim: Changes in brain PER2 levels capture more of the acute IEG effects than in the periphery because sleep-wake states are brain states.
source: As sleep-wake states are brain states, it stands to reason that changes in brain PER2 levels capture more of the acute IEG effects than in the periphery.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of tissue-specific differences.

claim: Changes in bioluminescence during baseline and after a 6 hr SD reflect changes in PER2 protein as validated by western blot.
source: Using western blot, we previously validated that changes in bioluminescence during baseline and after a 6 hr SD indeed reflect changes in PER2 protein (Curie et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Curie et al., 2015.

claim: The expression of two clock genes known to oscillate in anti-phase could be confirmed using osmotic mini-pumps for luciferin delivery.
source: Arguments against a possible temperature effect on bioluminescence changes come from a study in which, using the same osmotic mini-pumps, the expression of two clock genes known to oscillate in anti-phase could be confirmed (Ono et al., 2015)
evidence: This is cited from Ono et al., 2015.

claim: The circadian rhythm in wakefulness in the CAG-Luc and Pkg1-Luc mice was not accompanied by changes in bioluminescence.
source: In the current data, the circadian rhythm in wakefulness in the CAG-Luc and Pkg1-Luc mice was not accompanied by changes in bioluminescence.
evidence: This is stated in the text as evidence against temperature effects on bioluminescence.

claim: The lack of an increase in bioluminescence during wake bouts in Pkg1-Luc mice demonstrates that changes in rate-limiting availability of luciferin did not contribute to the fast sleep-wake-evoked changes in PER2.
source: Moreover, the lack of an increase in bioluminescence during wake bouts in Pkg1-Luc mice demonstrates that changes in rate-limiting availability of luciferin did not contribute to the fast sleep-wake-evoked changes in PER2.
evidence: This is stated in the text as evidence against luciferin availability effects.

claim: The sleep-wake distribution profoundly affects PER2 bioluminescence both short and long term.
source: In this study, we used a unique combination of methods allowing us to collect high-resolution data of sleep-wake state in conjunction with PER2 levels and found that the sleep-wake distribution profoundly affects PER2 bioluminescence both short and long term.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Behavior-dependent plasticity of the time-keeping machinery in tissues peripheral to the SCN enables the organism to respond to challenges as time-restricted feeding experiments have demonstrated.
source: Such behavior-dependent plasticity of the time-keeping machinery in tissues peripheral to the SCN enables the organism to respond to challenges as time-restricted feeding experiments have demonstrated (Damiola et al., 2000; Saini et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Damiola et al., 2000 and Saini et al., 2013.

claim: The clock circuitry plays a prominent role in sleep homeostasis.
source: Besides its importance in regulating feeding and energy homeostasis (Bass and Takahashi, 2010), the clock circuitry also plays a prominent role in sleep homeostasis (Franken, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Bass and Takahashi, 2010 and Franken, 2013.

claim: PER2 is sensitive to a variety of sleep-wake-driven signals, making it suited as an integrator of sleep-wake state and circadian time.
source: PER2 seems perfectly suited as an integrator of sleep-wake state and circadian time because it is sensitive to a variety of sleep-wake-driven signals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Having a large amplitude rhythm protects from acute disturbances of sleep as observed in the 2hOnOff experiment.
source: Our model suggests that having a large amplitude rhythm protects from acute disturbances of sleep as observed in the 2hOnOff experiment
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling analysis.

claim: Sleep-depriving arrhythmic SCNx mice had immediate and large effects on PER2.
source: while sleep-depriving arrhythmic SCNx mice had immediate and large effects on PER2.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a finding from the study.

claim: The coordination of the sleep-wake force and the second force in the model was critical in predicting the effects of sleep-wake interventions on PER2.
source: The coordination of the sleep-wake force and this second force in the model was critical in predicting the effects of sleep-wake interventions on PER2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling analysis.
